docs.title: About
docs.text:
My name is Justin Cassidy, and I am a Grade 12 student who is especially interested in software engineering and robotics. I am taking Engineering II because I enjoy technology, solving problems, and learning new things.

Outside of class, I run a local ultimate frisbee pickup group, which has taught me a lot about leadership and teamwork. I hope to keep building my skills in software and robotics as I prepare for future studies and projects.

docs.title: 1. Summary
docs.text:
• Goal: build a hot-wire styrofoam cutter using nichrome wire for smooth, easy cuts.
  • Purpose: make set building for school plays faster and more precise.
  • Designs:
  • Table version – base + overhead arm, nichrome wire hangs vertically.
  • Handheld version – T-shaped handle with stretched wire at the end.
  • Power: wired to run voltage through nichrome, heating it enough to cut foam.

docs.title: 2. Problems + Solutions
docs.text:
• Wire elongation when hot → added a spring (table) or flexible sticks (handheld) to keep tension.
  • Risk of burning wood → positioned wiring so only the nichrome section heated.
  • Indecisiveness / stalling → solved by sticking to deadlines and just building to test ideas.
  • Weak, brittle wood → learned to pre-drill holes before inserting screws.

docs.title: 3. What I Learned
docs.text:
• Technical skills:
  • First time soldering.
  • More precise wood cutting and drilling.
  • Importance of pre-drilling to avoid splitting.
  • Non-technical lessons:
  • Delegation and task management are key.
  • Sometimes you need to stop overthinking and just build.

docs.title: Reflection on Building the Class Project Site
Project Summary
docs.text: This class project I built a simple website and threw it up on GitHub. At first, I had no clue what I was doing—picture a lost tourist with a backpack full of basic instuctions—but somehow I made it work, one step (and error message) at a time.

docs.title: Challenges I Faced
docs.text:
• Trial and error was basically my best friend.
  • Uploading to GitHub? Half the time I wondered if I was pushing code or just shouting into the void.

docs.title: What I Learned
docs.text:
• GitHub is actually useful (and not a mysterious black hole).
  • I can upload, manage, and keep track of files without too much drama.
  • Markdown is magic for formatting.
  • Lifesaver resource: Markdown Cheat Sheet.

docs.title: Reflection & Next Steps
docs.text: Perseverance is key. Sometimes you need to do “dumb” experiments, break stuff, and keep going until it finally works. Next time I want to: - Plan my site layout before diving in. - Learn version control commands so I can work with more flow. - Add cooler styling and features once I am braver with CSS.

docs.title: 😑 Conclusion
docs.text: This project taught me that tools like GitHub and Markdown are actually fun once you get them down. More importantly, it reminded me that not giving up turns frustration into small victor

docs.title: Creating a new project
docs.text:
If you are tryinig to create a new project wtih uv: 

mkdir newProjectName
dc newProjectName

uv init -p 3.13

uv add yourPackageHere
uv run python main.py

docs.title: Project Recovery
docs.text:
If you want to bring your project down from GitHub into a new folder on your computer, use:

# Replace the link with YOUR repo’s URL
git clone https://github.com/USERNAME/REPOSITORY-NAME.git

cd repoName
uv sync

docs.title: Creating a new project w/ PIP
docs.text:
If you want to crate a new project and you hate yourself, you can use pip. 

# Create a virtual enviorment
python -m venv .venv
#Enter into the virtual enviorment
.venv\Scripts\activate
pip install yourPackigesHere

#Write your code and then
python main.py

docs.title: Project Recovery w/ pip
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/USERNAME/REPOSITORY-NAME.git

cd repoName
pip install -r requirements.txt

Also here is how to send stuff to update on Github

uv run mkdocs gh-deploy
